Icelandic Tariff Hike on Logistics Equipment Raises Industry Concerns

Reykjavik – The Icelandic government’s newly imposed tariff on imported logistics equipment is sending ripples through the nation’s Transportation & Logistics industry, with operators warning of higher costs, supply disruptions, and delayed infrastructure upgrades.

Announced last week and taking effect immediately, the 18% tariff applies to a range of specialized equipment including cargo handling machinery, refrigerated containers, and fleet maintenance parts. The measure was introduced in response to what the Ministry of Finance called “a need to strengthen domestic supply chains and encourage local manufacturing.” However, industry stakeholders say the sudden move has caught them off guard and is already affecting operations.

“We rely on imported pallet trucks, vehicle lifts, and container systems—there simply isn’t local production for these complex items,” said Brynjar Einarsson, CEO of Reykjavik Port Logistics. “The tariff is adding significant costs to ongoing contracts, and we’re seeing suppliers hesitate to dispatch orders while they recalculate prices. This is putting pressure on our ability to deliver goods across the country efficiently.”

According to the Icelandic Association of Transport Operators, the tariff has led to an average 12% increase in procurement costs for logistics firms over the past week. The association’s chair, Hafdís Jónsdóttir, warned that if the measure remains in place, “We may soon see higher shipping fees for domestic businesses and delays in rolling out new or replacement vehicles and equipment.”

Several regional distribution hubs, including those operated by Norðurljós Freight and Fjallabakki Transports, report that shipments of essential parts for vehicle fleets have been postponed or rerouted. “We’re juggling schedules and cannibalizing working equipment to keep our trucks on the road,” said Árni Stefánsson, maintenance manager at Norðurljós Freight’s Akureyri depot. “If this continues, it could disrupt supply lines, especially to rural areas.”

Industry analysts suggest that the measure could also undermine Iceland’s efforts to modernize its transport infrastructure. “Logistics is the backbone of the country’s economy, given our geography,” noted Rósa Magnúsdóttir, a trade policy consultant based in Reykjavik. “This tariff, while intended to promote domestic manufacturing, could slow down investment in state-of-the-art equipment and make local companies less competitive.”

Government officials maintain that the policy is under review and that dialogue with industry representatives is ongoing. “We are monitoring the effects closely and remain open to adjustments,” said Ólafur Sigurðsson, spokesperson for the Ministry of Finance.

As the tariff remains in effect, logistics operators across Iceland are bracing for continued challenges, with many calling for swift reassessment to prevent further strain on the sector.
